headline: Alder Compliance's numbers check out against independent estimates on every point the research can reach, and the deck names its own biggest risk before an investor has to — the open question is whether depth beats two well-funded leaders moving down-market, not whether the founders are being straight.

verdict.confidence_rationale: Every verifiable claim in the deck is supported by the research: market size, growth, serviceable slice, competitive framing, retention and CAC payback all fall inside the independently estimated bands [S1][S2][S3]. Confidence is medium rather than high because the deck omits the team entirely and never defines the 'depth' its whole differentiation rests on, so the two things that would decide the investment are the two things not in evidence.

scorecard.rationale: The deck says $2.8B in 2025 growing roughly 22%; independent estimates put compliance automation at $2.6-3.0B for 2025 with growth of 20-24% [S1]. The serviceable slice the deck claims — startups between Series A and Series C in North America, 'closer to $340M' — sits inside the $300-400M the research gives for that same segment [S1]. The sizing is accurate. The score is a 6 rather than higher because an accurate $340M is still a small market to build a fund-returning outcome in.
evidence: Deck slide 3: $2.8B in 2025, ~22% growth, $340M serviceable slice
Compliance automation $2.6-3.0B for 2025, 20-24% growth, Series A-C North America segment $300-400M [S1]

scorecard.rationale: The deck's characterisation is correct: Vanta and Drata are the two clear leaders, both heavily funded [S2]. It is also correct that open-source alternatives exist for control monitoring but do not produce auditor-ready evidence packages [S2] — the deck says this almost verbatim. What the deck states as a future risk, the research reports as already underway: both leaders have been extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies [S2]. Competing on price and depth against two well-funded leaders already moving into your segment is a hard position honestly described.
evidence: Vanta and Drata are the two clear leaders, heavily funded, both extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies; open-source exists for control monitoring but not auditor-ready evidence [S2]

scorecard.rationale: 'Depth for a narrower customer profile' is the entire differentiation and it is never defined. The deck concedes on slide 6 that depth is 'defensible but not permanent', which is the right reading, but an undefined differentiator cannot be assessed for durability. No product mechanism is described anywhere.
evidence: No product description in the deck

scorecard.rationale: The deck competes on price and never states a price. CAC payback of 14 months is given and sits inside the 12-18 month normal band for this category [S3]. $520k ARR across 41 customers implies roughly $12.7k each, which is arithmetic on the deck's behalf rather than a stated figure. No gross margin.
evidence: CAC payback of 12-18 months is within the normal band [S3]

scorecard.rationale: The most complete traction slide of any deck of this size: $520k ARR, 41 customers, 8% MoM sustained over six months, 104% net revenue retention, 14-month CAC payback. Six months of growth history is long enough to be a trend rather than a spike, and giving retention unprompted is unusual. The one qualification is that 104% NRR is typical rather than distinguishing — above 100% is normal for compliance vendors serving growing startups, since customers add frameworks over time [S3]. So it confirms the business is healthy; it does not by itself demonstrate an edge.
evidence: NRR above 100% is typical for compliance vendors serving growing startups; CAC payback 12-18 months is normal [S3]

scorecard.rationale: No team slide, no founders, no headcount, no advisors. Nothing was supplied to assess. In a deck that is otherwise unusually forthcoming, this omission stands out.
evidence: No team information in the deck

scorecard.rationale: $4M at $20M post is $16M pre on $520k ARR, roughly 31x — high but not unusual, and lower than most decks at this stage attempt. Unlike most, this one states the milestone: $2M ARR in 24 months. From $520k at 8% MoM that is achievable well inside the window if the rate holds, which makes it a checkable promise rather than an aspiration. Use of funds is still missing.
evidence: Deck slide 7: $4M at $20M post to reach $2M ARR in 24 months
Deck slide 5: 8% MoM for six months

claim_audit.claim: The compliance automation market was $2.8B in 2025 growing at roughly 22% a year according to independent analyst estimates
claim_audit.market_evidence: Independent estimates put compliance automation at $2.6-3.0B for 2025 with growth of 20-24% annually [S1].
claim_audit.delta: $2.8B is the midpoint of the $2.6-3.0B range and 22% is inside the 20-24% band. No material gap.
claim_audit.so_what: The market slide can be taken at face value, which is rare enough to be a signal in itself about how this team handles numbers.

claim_audit.claim: Our serviceable slice — startups between Series A and Series C in North America — is closer to $340M
claim_audit.market_evidence: The startup segment between Series A and Series C in North America is plausibly $300-400M [S1].
claim_audit.delta: $340M sits inside $300-400M, and the segment definition the deck uses matches the one the research sizes.
claim_audit.so_what: The serviceable market is honestly stated. It is also small: $340M is the ceiling on the whole segment, not on this company.

claim_audit.claim: Vanta and Drata dominate this category and are both well funded
claim_audit.market_evidence: Vanta and Drata are the two clear leaders in compliance automation, both heavily funded [S2].
claim_audit.delta: None. The deck names its two strongest competitors and concedes their position.
claim_audit.so_what: A competition slide that concedes rather than dismisses is a different underwriting object from one that names spreadsheets.

claim_audit.claim: Open-source tooling exists but does not produce auditor-ready evidence
claim_audit.market_evidence: Open-source alternatives exist for control monitoring but do not produce auditor-ready evidence packages [S2].
claim_audit.delta: None. The deck's characterisation matches the research closely.
claim_audit.so_what: It also identifies where the commercial value actually sits — the evidence package, not the monitoring — which is the more durable half of the product.

claim_audit.market_evidence: Net revenue retention above 100% is typical for compliance vendors serving growing startups, as customers add frameworks over time [S3].
claim_audit.delta: 104% is above 100% and therefore normal for the category. It is at the low end of what 'typical' implies rather than a standout.
claim_audit.so_what: Confirms health, does not demonstrate an edge. Worth asking how much of the 4% is framework expansion versus seat growth.

claim_audit.market_evidence: CAC payback of 12-18 months is within the normal band for compliance software [S3].
claim_audit.delta: 14 months sits in the middle of the normal band.
claim_audit.so_what: Efficient enough that the $4M can be spent on growth rather than on fixing acquisition.

claim_audit.claim: Vanta could move down-market at any time
claim_audit.market_evidence: Both Vanta and Drata have been extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies [S2].
claim_audit.delta: The risk the deck states as conditional is reported by the research as already in progress, and it applies to both leaders rather than one.
claim_audit.so_what: The deck is right about the mechanism and behind on the timing. That moves this from a risk to monitor to a condition to test now.

claim_audit.claim: $520k ARR across 41 customers, 8% MoM growth for six months
claim_audit.market_evidence: No source addresses this company's revenue.
claim_audit.delta: Cannot be checked externally. Internally consistent and well specified for the stage.
claim_audit.so_what: Diligence item, and an easy one given the level of detail already offered.

claim_audit.claim: Collecting SOC2 evidence takes an engineer roughly six weeks of part-time work spread over a quarter
claim_audit.delta: Plausible and specific; nothing in the research speaks to it.
claim_audit.so_what: Ask whether it comes from customer data or from the founders' own experience.

claim_audit.claim: Raising $4M at $20M post to reach $2M ARR in 24 months
claim_audit.market_evidence: No source addresses valuations in this category.
claim_audit.delta: About 31x ARR. The milestone is arithmetically reachable from $520k at the stated 8% MoM.
claim_audit.so_what: The plan is checkable, which is more than most decks offer. Whether 31x is the right price is a judgment the research does not settle.

where_deck_matches_market: Serviceable slice: $340M claimed, $300-400M estimated for the same segment definition [S1].
Competitive framing: Vanta and Drata named as dominant and well funded, which the research confirms [S2].
Open source: exists for control monitoring, does not produce auditor-ready evidence — stated by the deck and by the research in nearly the same terms [S2].
Retention and payback: 104% NRR and 14-month payback both sit inside the category's normal bands [S3].
where_deck_overstates: Nothing material. On every claim the research can reach, the deck is inside the independently estimated range.
where_deck_understates: The competitive timing. The deck presents Vanta moving down-market as something that 'could' happen; the research reports both leaders already extending toward earlier-stage companies [S2]. Understating a threat is less common than overstating an opportunity and is worth naming as the one place the deck is behind the evidence.
Its own credibility. A deck whose every number survives checking has earned an argument it never makes.

blind_spots.what: Both Vanta and Drata — not just Vanta — have already been extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The deck treats this as a future risk from one competitor. It is a present condition from both, and it compresses the window in which 'depth for a narrower profile' remains available as a position.

blind_spots.what: 104% NRR is typical rather than distinguishing, because compliance customers add frameworks as they grow.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The deck presents retention as evidence of product strength. The research says the category gets that lift structurally, so 104% shows the business is behaving normally rather than outperforming — and at the low end of normal.

blind_spots.what: The $340M serviceable slice is the whole segment, and it is the ceiling.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The deck is right about the number but never confronts what it implies: reaching $2M ARR takes 0.6% of the segment, which is achievable, but a fund-returning outcome requires either a share of that market that no fourth player usually gets, or expansion beyond the segment the deck has defined. Neither is addressed.

risks.risk: Vanta and Drata complete their move down-market and remove the price-and-depth position entirely
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask what has happened to win rate against each over the last two quarters, and at what price [S2].

risks.risk: 'Depth' is a feature set rather than a moat and is matched within a release cycle
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask the founders to name the three things they do that Vanta cannot, and check each against Vanta's current product.

risks.risk: The $340M serviceable market caps the outcome below what the round needs to return
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask what the segment expansion path is beyond Series A-C North America [S1].

risks.risk: 104% NRR erodes as the customer base ages past the framework-addition phase
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask for NRR by cohort age rather than in aggregate [S3].

risks.risk: The team is unknown and may not be able to execute against two well-funded leaders
Competing on price against heavily funded leaders invites a price response they can absorb and Alder cannot
risks.mitigation_or_test: Ask what happens to the model if the price falls 30%.

questions: Both leaders are already extending down-market — what has that done to your win rate and price in the last two quarters? [S2]
Name the three things your depth does that Vanta cannot do today.
Your NRR is 104% and the category typically runs above 100% on framework additions — how much of yours is expansion versus framework attach? [S3]
$340M is the whole segment; what is the path beyond it? [S1]
Who is the team, and have they sold into this buyer before?
What is your actual price, given that price is half your stated differentiation?
Where does the six-weeks-of-engineering figure come from?
What does the $4M buy, and what happens to the 24-month plan if growth falls to 5% MoM?

actions.action: Request founder backgrounds — the single missing input on an otherwise checkable deck
Test the depth claim feature-by-feature against Vanta's current product
Get win/loss history against Vanta and Drata with prices, covering the down-market move [S2]
Reference three customers on why they chose Alder over the leaders
Model the outcome against a $340M segment ceiling and ask for the expansion thesis [S1]

summary:
Alder Compliance sells SOC2 evidence collection to startups approaching Series A. It has $520k ARR across 41 customers, 8% month-over-month growth sustained over six months, 104% net revenue retention and 14-month CAC payback, and is raising $4M at $20M post to reach $2M ARR in 24 months.

The unusual thing about this deck is that its numbers survive checking. It claims the compliance automation market was $2.8B in 2025 growing roughly 22%; independent estimates give $2.6-3.0B with 20-24% growth [S1]. It narrows to a serviceable slice of 'closer to $340M' for startups between Series A and Series C in North America; the research sizes that same segment at $300-400M [S1]. The narrowing itself is the right shape — a stated segment definition with a smaller number attached, rather than a percentage taken off a large one. Retention and payback both land inside the category's normal bands [S3].

The competition slide concedes rather than deflects. It names Vanta and Drata as dominant and well funded, which the research confirms [S2], and states that open-source tooling exists for control monitoring but does not produce auditor-ready evidence — almost exactly what the research says [S2]. Slide 6 then volunteers the single most dangerous risk to the business: that Vanta could move down-market, and that depth is defensible but not permanent. Very few decks name their own kill shot.

The research does correct the deck in one direction, and it is the direction that matters. Both Vanta and Drata have already been extending down-market toward earlier-stage companies [S2]. The deck treats this as a conditional future event from one competitor; it is a present condition from both. That does not make the deck dishonest — it makes it slightly behind, and it compresses the window in which a price-and-depth position remains available.

Two things temper the positive read. The first is that 104% NRR is typical rather than distinguishing: compliance vendors serving growing startups get retention lift structurally as customers add frameworks [S3], so 104% shows the business behaving normally, at the low end of normal, rather than outperforming. The second is that the deck is right about $340M without confronting what $340M implies. Reaching $2M ARR needs 0.6% of the segment and is plausible; a fund-returning outcome needs either a share a fourth entrant rarely gets, or an expansion path beyond the segment, and the deck offers neither.

Against all of that, the deck contains no team slide at all — no founders, no backgrounds, no headcount. In a deck this forthcoming, that omission is conspicuous, and at seed the team is most of what is being underwritten.

The call is YES WITH CONDITIONS. The single biggest reason to proceed is that everything checkable checks out, which is both a fact about the market and a signal about the founders. The conditions are specific: founder backgrounds, and a feature-level defence of 'depth' against Vanta's current product together with win/loss data covering the period in which both leaders moved down-market [S2]. What would flip it to a pass is discovering that depth is a feature list rather than a structural advantage, or that win rates against the leaders have already started to fall.
